expected_evidence: Geological: an ejecta/fallout stratigraphic layer at ~10,950 BCE (Younger Dryas Boundary) across multiple North American sites containing platinum and iridium anomalies, magnetic and glassy microspherules, and nanodiamonds/lonsdaleite consistent with impact or airburst fallout, often overlying a 'black mat' organic-rich layer.
Geological: shock-metamorphosed quartz grains, melt-glass, or other high-temperature/high-pressure mineral indicators near dated impact-age horizons.

Astronomical: evidence of an impactor source - a confirmed crater of matching age (candidates like the Hiawatha crater in Greenland have been proposed but not firmly dated to this event), or cosmic-dust/extraterrestrial-isotope signatures (He-3, nickel ratios) in the ejecta layer.

Material/archaeological: abrupt termination of Clovis-culture artifact horizons and megafaunal bone beds directly beneath or within the proposed impact layer, charcoal/soot layers indicating continent-wide wildfires coincident with the boundary.
Genetic: a sharp, dated population-collapse signature in ancient DNA of megafaunal taxa (mammoth, horse, etc.) clustering tightly around 10,950 BCE rather than a gradual decline.
Oral tradition/iconographic: purported Indigenous North American narratives or rock art motifs interpreted as memories of a sky-fire/flood event (highly speculative, low-confidence category).
response.rationale: The interval given (-10950) places this hypothesis at the Younger Dryas onset, so the 'younger-dryas' row is the appropriate detectability context despite the unspecified period label. The stated mechanism (impact-ejecta-fallout) points primarily to geological (0.65) and astronomical (0.7) evidence classes, both of which have comparatively high detectability scores in this table - chemically and mineralogically distinctive fallout layers (platinum/iridium spikes, spherules, nanodiamonds, black mats) are the kind of physical stratigraphic signal that plausibly survives ~13,000 years and is routinely sampled by geologists, so absence of such evidence would be harder to excuse on detectability grounds alone. Material (0.35) and genetic (0.3) lines are moderately detectable and have in fact been actively investigated in the literature. Textual (0.0) and linguistic (0.05) evidence are essentially impossible for this pre-literate North American context, and oral_tradition (0.1) and iconographic (0.1) evidence are very low-confidence categories given the ~13-millennium gap and risk of retrospective reinterpretation. Weighting toward the mechanism-relevant geological/astronomical classes while discounting the low-yield categories gives an overall adjustment around 0.55. Note (model-prior, unverified against the evidence text provided): my training-derived recollection is that the 'Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis' is a real, long-standing but strongly contested proposal in the literature - proponents have reported platinum, nanodiamond, and spherule anomalies at multiple North American sites, but numerous independent studies have failed to replicate these findings or have attributed them to non-impact processes (wildfire soot, algal-produced nanoparticles, sample contamination), and no confirmed dated impact crater has been established. This means that even though the relevant evidence classes are plausibly detectable, the 'corroborated' status of the hypothesis is empirically disputed rather than settled - so a low detectability score should not be invoked to explain away the absence of consensus evidence, since much of the claimed evidence does exist but its interpretation remains actively contested.
